---
title: "Why test, and what can be tested"
---

Every app you built this year you checked by hand: start it, click, look. That
works while the app is small and you still remember what it is supposed to do.
The bracelet editor from the last chapter already carries four rules, and
walking through all of them after every change costs a minute of clicking. A
test is that minute, written down once and run by a program in under a second.

There is a coding buddy for this part too, and tests are the thing it knows
that the Part 4 buddy did not. Its key goes into `~/.pi/agent/auth.json` in
place of the old one (@sec-buddy-setup-new-part).

{{< coding coding-buddy-tests >}}

## A test that fails on purpose {#sec-why-test-experiment}

From this part on your apps come from a second template: the starter you
already know with a test runner added.

1. Create a new app from the
   [vite-ts-starter-tests](https://github.com/Teaching-HTL-Leonding/vite-ts-starter-tests)
   template. Download the ZIP, unpack it into `coursework/` as `first-test`,
   open the folder in VS Code, and run `npm install`. Every later chapter says
   "create a new app from our tests template" and means this one.

2. Run `npm test`. The terminal answers like this (your path and the times
   differ, and Vitest prints a few more lines than this book quotes):

   ```text
    RUN  v4.1.11 /home/you/creative-coding-2/coursework/first-test


    Test Files  1 passed (1)
         Tests  1 passed (1)
      Start at  20:12:39
      Duration  156ms
   ```

Green, and you clicked nothing. Find out what ran. Open `src/math.ts`:

```ts
export function add(firstNumber: number, secondNumber: number): number {
  return firstNumber + secondNumber;
}
```

Next to it sits `src/math.test.ts`, which is the file `npm test` picked up:

```ts
import { describe, expect, it } from 'vitest';
import { add } from './math.ts';

describe('add', () => {
  it('adds two numbers', () => {
    expect(add(2, 3)).toBe(5);
  });
});
```

Read the middle line the way it is written: it adds two numbers, and you expect
`add(2, 3)` to be `5`.

3. Now break `add`. Change `firstNumber + secondNumber` to
   `firstNumber - secondNumber`, save, and run `npm test` again:

   ```text
    ❯ src/math.test.ts (1 test | 1 failed) 6ms
        × adds two numbers 5ms

    FAIL  src/math.test.ts > add > adds two numbers
   AssertionError: expected -1 to be 5 // Object.is equality

   - Expected
   + Received

   - 5
   + -1

    ❯ src/math.test.ts:6:23
         4| describe('add', () => {
         5|   it('adds two numbers', () => {
         6|     expect(add(2, 3)).toBe(5);
          |                       ^
         7|   });
         8| });


    Test Files  1 failed (1)
         Tests  1 failed (1)
   ```

   `AssertionError: expected -1 to be 5` is the whole story. Your `add` handed
   back `-1` where the test wanted `5`. The block underneath shows the exact
   line of the test file, with a caret under the call that disagreed.

4. Put the `+` back and run `npm test` once more. Green again, and you never
   opened the browser.

## What those three names do {#sec-why-test-names}

`expect(add(2, 3)).toBe(5)` is the comparison. `expect` takes the value your
code produced, and `toBe` is one of many ways to check it. This one compares
with `===`, the same operator you write in an `if`.

`it('adds two numbers', ...)` is one test. The string is its name, and it turns
up again in the `FAIL` line when the test goes red, which is why a name that
reads like a sentence is worth the two seconds it takes to write.

`describe('add', ...)` groups the tests that are about the same thing and puts
that group name in front of every failure. `add > adds two numbers` in the
output above is the group and the test.

A **unit test** is a small program that calls one piece of your code and
compares the answer with what you expected. The unit is that piece: one
function or one method, sometimes a whole class. Vitest is the program that
finds the test files and runs them. What it prints at the end is the score.

## Regressions and edge cases {#sec-why-test-why}

**A regression is working code that stops working because you changed something
somewhere else.** The bracelet's "Remove last" button and its mixed-color
warning have nothing to do with each other, right up to the day you edit the
array that both of them read. A suite of tests that runs in one second finds
that on the spot. Clicking finds it three weeks later, in a lesson about
something else.

**An edge case is the input at the border.** The empty bracelet, the first item,
the last item, zero, a negative number. Those are the cases hand testing skips,
because clicking your way back to an empty bracelet is boring and you are fairly
sure it works. Written down once as tests, they run again on every save for the
rest of the project.

## Node has no document {#sec-why-test-node}

Vitest runs your code in Node, not in a browser. Node has no page: no
`document`, no `<div>`, nothing to click. Point a test at code that touches the
page and Vitest answers with one line.

```text
ReferenceError: document is not defined
```

That message decides the shape of every project in this part. Your logic goes
into files that never mention `document`, and `src/index.ts` is the only file
that looks up elements and listens for events. It does all the drawing too.
Test files import the logic and never import `index.ts`.

Your bracelet from the last chapter breaks that rule twice over. `Bracelet`
takes the container element in its constructor, so a test cannot even create
one, and its private `render()` builds the `<div>`s. `LetterCube` and
`SpacerBead` have the same problem in miniature. The exercise below splits the
project: the classes keep the items and the rules, `index.ts` takes over all the
drawing, and only then is there something a test can reach.

## What the tests template adds {#sec-why-test-template}

`package.json` gains two development dependencies, `vitest` and
`@playwright/test`, plus three scripts:

```json
"test": "vitest run",
"test:watch": "vitest",
"test:e2e": "playwright test"
```

`npm test` runs every test once and exits, and that is the command of this part.
`npm run test:watch` stays open and runs the tests again after every save; the
next chapter puts it to work. `npm run test:e2e` starts Playwright, a second
test tool that drives a real browser, and Part 8 is where you meet it. Until
then `playwright.config.ts` and the `e2e/` folder stay as they are. The one
Playwright test in there checks the template's own page, so it goes red once you
write your own `index.html`, and nothing in this part runs it.

In `src/` you find the two files you just read, `math.ts` and `math.test.ts`. A
Vitest test file is named `*.test.ts` and lives next to the module it tests.
Playwright's files are named `e2e/*.e2e.ts`, so neither runner ever picks up the
other one's files.

Two smaller differences: `biome.json` also skips the `playwright-report` and
`test-results` folders, and `.gitignore` keeps both of them out of git.

One line in the template deserves a comment. Its test file imports with the file
extension:

```ts
import { add } from './math.ts';
```

Both spellings compile in these projects. This book writes imports without the
extension, the way Part 4 does it, and so does every file you write from here
on. The template's `src/index.ts` still carries the year-one
`getElementById(...) as ...` line, and you replace that file in every project
anyway. Everything else is the starter you toured in Part 2.

## Exercise: split the bracelet {#sec-why-test-exercise}

The bracelet editor keeps every rule it has and gains a `Bracelet` class you can
test.

{{< exercise bracelet tests=true >}}

1. Create a new app from our tests template inside `homework/`, in a folder
   called `bracelet-tests`.

2. Copy six files from your `homework/bracelet` project into the new `src/`:
   `bracelet-item.ts`, `letter-cube.ts`, `spacer-bead.ts`, `rule-error.ts`,
   `bracelet.ts`, and `index.ts`. Leave `rule-error.ts` exactly as it is; every
   other file changes in the steps below.

3. Open `src/bracelet-item.ts` and replace the abstract class with a type:

   ```ts
   import type { LetterCube } from './letter-cube';
   import type { SpacerBead } from './spacer-bead';

   export type BraceletItem = LetterCube | SpacerBead;
   ```

   The abstract class existed to promise one thing, `render()`, and that promise
   is moving out of the model. With no shared behavior left, a base class has
   nothing to hold, and a union type says "a letter cube or a spacer bead"
   just as well. `instanceof` still narrows it, which the next steps need.

4. Shrink `src/letter-cube.ts` to a class that only holds data:

   ```ts
   export class LetterCube {
     readonly letter: string;

     constructor(letter: string) {
       this.letter = letter;
     }
   }
   ```

   The `extends` clause and the whole `render()` method are gone, and the field
   is `readonly` and public, because `index.ts` has to read it to draw the cube.
   Do the same to `src/spacer-bead.ts` with `readonly color: string`.

5. Open `src/bracelet.ts`. Delete the container field, the constructor, and the
   private `render()` method, and delete every `this.render()` call inside
   `addLetter`, `addSpacer`, and `removeLast`. Rename the private array field to
   `itemList`, so that the name `items` is free for this getter:

   ```ts
   get items(): BraceletItem[] {
     return this.itemList.slice();
   }
   ```

   Called without arguments, `slice()` gives you a copy of the array, so
   whoever reads `bracelet.items` cannot push into the bracelet behind its
   back. Everything else in the class stays: both adding methods with their
   `RuleError`, `removeLast`, and the two private helpers.

6. Open `src/index.ts`. The bracelet no longer takes an argument, so create it
   with `new Bracelet()`, and add a drawing helper next to `showMessage`:

   ```ts
   const render = (): void => {
     braceletBox.replaceChildren();
     for (const item of bracelet.items) {
       const element = document.createElement('div');
       if (item instanceof LetterCube) {
         element.classList.add('cube');
         element.textContent = item.letter;
       } else {
         element.classList.add('bead');
         element.style.backgroundColor = item.color;
       }
       braceletBox.append(element);
     }
   };
   ```

   That needs `import { LetterCube } from './letter-cube';` at the top. Now call
   `render()` in every listener right after the model call, and once at the very
   end of the file so the empty bracelet is drawn when the page loads.

7. Delete `src/math.ts` and `src/math.test.ts`. The `index.html` you copied in
   has already replaced the template's page, so nothing looks for `add` any
   more.

8. Run `npm start` and try the editor. Expected results, the same as in the last
   chapter: a letter cube appears; a second letter right after it changes
   nothing and shows "You need to add a spacer bead next!"; a spacer bead on the
   empty bracelet shows "You need to add a letter cube next!"; a bead in a
   second color is added and shows "You are mixing spacer colors!" once and
   never again; "Remove last" takes items off one at a time.

9. Write your first test file, `src/bracelet.test.ts`, in the shape you read at
   the start of this chapter:

   ```ts
   import { describe, expect, it } from 'vitest';
   import { Bracelet } from './bracelet';

   describe('Bracelet', () => {
     it('starts with no items', () => {
       const bracelet = new Bracelet();
       expect(bracelet.items.length).toBe(0);
     });
   });
   ```

   Add a second `it` below the first one, named
   `'holds one item after the first letter'`. It creates a bracelet, calls
   `bracelet.addLetter('A')`, and expects `bracelet.items.length` to be `1`.

10. Run `npm test`. Expected output:

    ```text
     Test Files  1 passed (1)
          Tests  2 passed (2)
    ```

11. Add `"verify": "tsc --noEmit && biome check ."` to the `scripts` list in
    `package.json`, run `npm run verify`, fix what it reports, and commit.
